title: Action Potential Simulator
description: Interactive membrane-voltage vs time plot (mV, ms) for a simplified neuron model. Learners deliver single, paired, or held stimuli, block Na+ channels with lidocaine, and change outside K+ to explore threshold, the all-or-none principle, absolute and relative refractory periods, firing rate coding, and depolarization block. A side panel shows Na+ and K+ channel states.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: Neuroscience
learningObjectives: Predict whether a stimulus of a given strength will reach threshold and fire an action potential.
Explain why every action potential reaches the same peak (all-or-none principle).
Predict whether a second stimulus will fire during the absolute or relative refractory period.
Describe how a stronger steady stimulus increases firing rate without increasing spike size.
Predict the effect of blocking voltage-gated Na+ channels with lidocaine.
Explain how raising outside K+ shifts the resting potential and can first increase, then abolish, excitability.
prerequisites: Reading a line graph with labeled axes and units
keyQuestions: What is the weakest stimulus that fires a spike, and why does a stronger one not make a bigger spike?
Why does a second stimulus fail if it comes too soon after the first?
How does a neuron signal a stronger stimulus if every spike is the same size?
Why does lidocaine stop action potentials?
Why does high outside K+ first make a neuron easier to fire and then impossible to fire?
misconceptions: A stronger stimulus produces a bigger action potential.
The sodium-potassium pump causes the falling phase of each spike.
Crossing the threshold line always produces a spike, even when Na+ channels are blocked.
A neuron can fire again immediately after a spike if the stimulus is strong enough.
simulationModel: Simplified phenomenological model, not full Hodgkin-Huxley. Subthreshold membrane is a leaky integrator (time constant 5 ms). Resting potential from the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz voltage equation at 37 C (K+ inside 140 mM, Na+ inside 15 mM, Na+ outside 145 mM, PNa/PK = 0.042). Spike fires at V >= -55 mV when enough Na+ channels are available; fixed-shape spike to +35 mV, repolarization to an undershoot near -80 mV, then recovery as K+ channels close (time constant 4 ms). Na+ inactivation recovers with a 2 ms time constant, producing absolute and relative refractory periods. Lidocaine modeled as blocking 85% of Na+ channels.
